messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 78
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Librarian
- Trauma Type: Terrorism
- Pcl5: 69

He sits on the edge of the leather chair in my office, his posture rigid, palms flat against his knees. At seventy-eight, a man of African heritage who spent his formative years in a city still imprinted on his nervous system, he moves with a deliberate care, as if the air itself might fracture. The memories of that afternoon still arrive unbidden, sharp and unrelenting. Thirty-four years ago, he walks home from the university library, a stack of borrowed monographs tucked under his arm. The world turns white. A tearing, rhythmic roar swallows the chatter of the square. When the dust settles, the cobblestones are painted in dark, wet patches. He pulls a stranger from the rubble before the sirens begin. He tells me this now without flinching, but his breath hitches on the word stranger. In the decades that follow, he builds a life on quiet routines. He becomes a librarian, drawn to the way books wait patiently for their readers, how they demand order and reward patience. He spends forty years cataloging histories he can never fully escape. His wife, Amara, knows the rhythm of his silence. She has learned not to startle him when he drops a cup, nor to press when he suddenly stops mid-sentence, his eyes fixed on a crack in the ceiling. She knows he checks the locks three times before bed, that he scans every room before she leaves, that he sleeps with the television on at low volume, just to drown out the hollow spaces. Today, he describes the present with the same measured cadence. He wakes at 3 a.m., as he does most nights, his chest tight. The ceiling fan’s click reads as a detonation to his nervous system. He gets up, pours water, and stands by the window watching the streetlights flicker. His hands tremble slightly until he counts the panes in the glass. He avoids the news, though he once devoured it daily, seeking patterns in the chaos. Now he turns the page of a newspaper only to fold it shut immediately, the headlines feeling too heavy, too close to the ones that live behind his eyelids. At the library, he works the rare books collection. The work grounds him. The smell of aging paper, the careful brushing of dust from spines, the quiet cataloging of provenance—it creates a perimeter he can trust. But when the fire alarm drills sound, his pen drops. His heart hammers against his ribs, and for a terrifying moment, the reading room dissolves back into that square of smoke and screaming. He has learned to breathe through it, to name the objects around him—a chair, a desk, a lamp—until the floor stops tilting. He returns to his desk, but the margin he was working on remains blank. He speaks of his wife with a quiet, enduring fondness, yet admits he keeps her at a careful distance, fearing his own fragility will contaminate her peace. He watches her sleep, memorizing the rise and fall of her shoulder, convinced that if he closes his eyes too long, the old alarms will sound again. He sits now in my office, fingers tracing the edge of a wooden table, his gaze resting on the door handle. He is here, in this room, in this moment, but part of him remains on those cobblestones, still waiting for the dust to clear. He breathes slowly, deliberately, and waits for me to speak.
